title: Dose Response graphs in R
text:
Introduction
This tutorial covers how to go from raw data in a Leishmania PrestoBlue assay to generating a dose-response curve and calculating IC50 values.
The R code will be very similar for each plate, so we can set it up so there’s only a few things we need to change for each one.

title: 2  Set up Posit Cloud workspace, upload the CSV file, and create an R file.
text:
Create a free account with Posit Cloud and sign in. You will not need a paid account for this work
Then:

Click "New Project" -> "New RStudio Project" and wait for this to load
Click the Upload button (under Files) and upload your CSV file.
Click the New File icon -> R Script
Click the Save icon and give the file a name

You are now set up to start coding in R.

title: 3  Read the CSV file into R
text:
In R, the first line of code will be to read the CSV file.
You will want to use headers = TRUE so that the first row is saved as the column headers.
You will need to put in your filename where it says "Test_data.csv"
Any text after a # is a comment - a note to ourselves to remind us what the code does.

# Read the CSV file into R, and name it raw_data
raw_data <- read.csv("Test_data.csv", header = TRUE)

You can run the code by highlighting the line and clicking “Run”
raw_data should then appear in your Environment - you can click this to view the table.
Check your column headings are what you expect them to be and that there aren’t any extra (empty) table cells!



Read the CSV file in R

title: 4  Calculate the control values (Blank, Live cells, DMSO)
text:
4.1 Calculating the blank
We can use the function mean() to calculate the average of a set of numbers. We can use $ to select the column of our dataframe, and [1:3] to select rows 1-3 (or any numbers).
If both rows of the blank are media only (Blank_L and Blank_R) you can calculate the blank with the line:
Blank_Average <- mean(mean(raw_data$Blank_L), mean(raw_data$Blank_R))
If you have some of your wells as a media and drug control, we can calculate the blank values separately for the different controls:
# Media only control in rows 1-3 of Blank_L
Blank_Average <- mean(raw_data$Blank_L[1:3])

# If you have a media + drug (no cells control), e.g. in rows 4-6 of Blank_L
Media_drug1_control <- mean(raw_data$Blank_L[4:6])
crumbs: 4  Calculate the control values (Blank, Live cells, DMSO)

title: 4  Calculate the control values (Blank, Live cells, DMSO)
text:
4.2 Calculating the Live/ DMSO controls
You can then calculate the Live and DMSO controls using these:

# Calculate Live cells average  (Live.DMSO rows 1-3)
Live_cells <- mean(raw_data$Live.DMSO[1:3]) - Blank_Average

# Calculate DMSO control average (Live.DMSO rows 4-6)
DMSO_cells <- mean(raw_data$Live.DMSO[4:6]) - Blank_Average
crumbs: 4  Calculate the control values (Blank, Live cells, DMSO)

title: 5  Define drug information, concentrations and locations
text:
For each drug, you’ll want to include the name, concentrations, locations and which blank to use. Once you have this information, you can use the provided functions to calculate the IC50 and draw the dose-response curve.
You can copy the below code and add in your values, concentrations etc.
Keep the variables as AmpB, Drug1 and Drug2 as we’ll use these in the next step.

# Data for AmpB
AmpB <- list(name = "Amphotericin B", 
          start_conc = 1.8, 
          unit = "µM",
          dilution_factor = 3, 
          col_start = 3, 
          col_stop = 5, 
          blank = Blank_Average, 
          positive_control = Live_cells)

# Data for Drug 1
Drug1 <- list(name = "Caffeic Acid", 
             start_conc = 277.5, 
             unit = "µM",
             dilution_factor = 2, 
             col_start = 6, 
             col_stop = 8, 
             blank = Blank_Average, 
             positive_control = DMSO_cells)

# Data for Drug 2 
Drug2 <- list(name = "CD9", 
             start_conc = 141.32, 
             unit = "µM",
             dilution_factor = 2, 
             col_start = 9, 
             col_stop = 11, 
             blank = Blank_Average, 
             positive_control = DMSO_cells)

See the below table for an explanation of each value.

title: 6  Make your IC50 calculations and Dose Response graphs
text:
6.1 Install packages
First you’ll need to install the packages needed:
# Install packages
install.packages("ggplot2")
install.packages("drc")

title: 6  Make your IC50 calculations and Dose Response graphs
section: 6.2 Copy and run the below code
text:
6.2 Copy and run the below code
Now all of the setup for your plate is done, the rest we can use the same code for each one.
See the screencast below the code for how to use:
In this example, the ggplot graph doesn’t calculate correctly for AmpB, this is to do with the variability in the data as viability decreases for the first few dilutions

# Import libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(drc)

# Define functions
calculate_dilutions <- function(highest_conc, dilution_factor, dilutions=5){
  result_vector <- highest_conc / (dilution_factor^(0:dilutions))  
  return(result_vector)
}

plot_publication_curve <- function(drug, raw_data_matrix) {
  
  # Extract data points for the chosen drug, using col_start and col_stop to select columns (all rows)
  drug_raw_data <- raw_data_matrix[, drug$col_start:drug$col_stop]
  
  # Calculate drug concentrations for each row using start concentration and dilution factor
  concs <- calculate_dilutions(drug$start_conc, drug$dilution_factor, dilutions = 5)
  
  # Make a big table with each concentration repeated for each raw value
  drug_data <- data.frame(
    conc = rep(concs, times = ncol(drug_raw_data)),
    raw_val = unlist(drug_raw_data)
  )
  
  # Minus blank, and divide by positive control, to get % viability
  drug_data$viability <- ((drug_data$raw_val - drug$blank) / drug$positive_control) * 100
  
  # Use drm from drc package to fit a dose-response curve to the data
  max_viability <- max(drug_data$viability)
  drug_model <- drm(viability ~ conc, data = drug_data, fct = LL.4(fixed = c(NA, 0, max_viability, NA)))  
  
  # print the results 
  print(summary(drug_model))
  
  # calculate and print the IC50 value
  ic50_info <- ED(drug_model, 50, type = "absolute", display = FALSE)
  cat("IC50 value: ", ic50_info[1], " with standard error ", ic50_info[2], "\n")
  
  # plot this dose-response model using Base R 
  plot(drug_model, broken = TRUE, type = "all", xlab = paste0(drug$name, " (",drug$unit,")"), ylab = "Percent viability")
  dose_curve_baseR <- recordPlot()
  
  # Use the model to create a set of predicted values, to use as a curve in a ggplot 
  prediction_data <- expand.grid(conc=seq(from=min(concs), to=max(concs), length = 100))
  pm <- predict(drug_model, newdata=prediction_data, interval="confidence")

  prediction_data$p <- pm[,1]
  prediction_data$pmin <- pm[,2]
  prediction_data$pmax <- pm[,3]
  
  xlabel <- paste0(drug$name, " (",drug$unit,")")
  
  # plot this with ggplot
  dose_curve_ggplot <- ggplot(drug_data, aes(x = conc, y = viability)) + 
    # plot the raw values, add scatter points
    geom_point() + 
    # add a ribbon using the predicted values
    geom_ribbon(data=prediction_data, aes(x=conc, y=p, ymin=pmin, ymax=pmax), alpha = 0.2) + 
    geom_line(data=prediction_data, aes(x=conc, y=p)) +
    # make the x axis a log scale
    scale_x_log10() + 
    # x and y axis labels
    xlab(xlabel) + ylab("Percent viability (cm)") + 
    theme_minimal()
    
    
  # return the values 
  return(list(IC50 = ic50_info, baseR = dose_curve_baseR, ggplot = dose_curve_ggplot)) 
}

# Run the functions for each graph
AmpB_graphs <- plot_publication_curve(AmpB, raw_data)
AmpB_graphs$IC50
AmpB_graphs$baseR
AmpB_graphs$ggplot

Drug1_graphs <- plot_publication_curve(Drug1, raw_data)
Drug1_graphs$IC50 
Drug1_graphs$baseR
Drug1_graphs$ggplot

Drug2_graphs <- plot_publication_curve(Drug2, raw_data)
Drug2_graphs$IC50
Drug2_graphs$baseR
Drug2_graphs$ggplot

title: 6  Make your IC50 calculations and Dose Response graphs
text:
6.3 Get the result
Each of the lines at the bottom will give you a different result:

AmpB_graphs$IC50: The IC50 value and standard error for Amphotericin B
AmpB_graphs$baseR: A simple dose-response curve
AmpB_graphs$ggplot: A fancier dose-response curve (which doesn’t work for AmpB in this example)

Once you’ve run the whole code, you can select and run one of these lines at a time.
The IC50 values will appear in the console, and the plots will appear in the bottom right panel. You can export the plots as PNG files.
